claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 at.% aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The aluminum addition will promote formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
Aluminum preferentially oxidizes at high temperature to form Al2O3.
A continuous Al2O3 scale acts as a diffusion barrier that reduces oxygen ingress into the alloy matrix.
Reduced oxygen ingress limits further oxidation and degradation of the bulk alloy.
The proposed aluminum addition should be beneficial at approximately 1200°C in ambient air for an exposure of about 10 hours.
The aluminum-doped alloy will develop a thinner oxide scale than the untreated alloy under the specified conditions.
The oxide scale on the aluminum-doped alloy will be more stable than that on the untreated alloy.
The aluminum-doped alloy will undergo less oxidation-induced material loss than the untreated alloy.
An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy forms a less protective oxide layer, resulting in greater oxygen uptake and material degradation.
Oxygen and nitrogen impurities can promote phase segregation and progressive softening during thermal aging of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
If the aluminum content is too low to form a continuous protective layer, the beneficial oxidation-resistance effect may not occur.
The benefit may disappear outside the temperature or oxygen-potential range in which an alumina scale remains stable.
Scale spallation at temperatures higher than 1200°C may eliminate the beneficial effect of aluminum.
